# The repair pass cannot see the panes the recovery kept alive for it

> ## ⚠️ NARROWED BY THE AUTHOR, 2026-09-05 — the behavioural claim below is WITHDRAWN
>
> **This ticket is now AC-4 only: a documentation defect.** The Problem section asserts that the
> recovery's preserved panes are orphaned and rebuilt in practice. **Three attempts never witnessed
> that, and in both runs that ever reached an assertion, pane identity SURVIVED.** The disposition to
> narrow was published here after attempt 2 and is being honoured rather than quietly extended.
>
> What still stands, because it never depended on a run: `settleFailedProjection`'s JSDoc promised
> *"the repair re-projection re-parents those panes by identity"*, and no mechanism that method
> controls delivers it. That is a guarantee in prose with nothing behind it — corrected in the diff.
>
> **Read the Problem section below as the hypothesis that motivated the work, not as established
> behaviour.** The three attempts and the fixture obstacle that blocked each are recorded in the
> parked spec and the closing commit, so a successor does not re-derive them.

## Context

Found while driving `#18275`, and it is the one claim that survived that ticket's night. I published a witness for a "retired-staged-shell duplicate" and then retracted the framing: measured at N, the arm was 1/12 red in one sample and 9/12 in another on the same code and command, and a probe suggesting identity-stable resolution removed it was withdrawn at Fisher exact 0.10 against a baseline whose own variance spans that range.

What never depended on either measurement is a source read, re-verified at `origin/dev` today: **the failed-projection recovery deliberately keeps live panes alive on a documented promise, and the code that is supposed to keep that promise cannot see them.** That is a static contract contradiction. It needs no flaky arm to state and none to fix.

This is filed separately from `#18275` rather than folded into it, deliberately — see Out of Scope.

The three facts the argument rests on were re-read at source and are unchanged: the default `resolvePane` still returns a fresh config literal, `resolveProjectedPane` still consults `returningTearOutPanes` first, and the failure still routes through `onDockProjectionFailed`. `Reconciler.mjs` was not touched by that merge, so its references are original.

## The Problem

A dock projection stages a second shell, moves live pane/button pairs into it, then commits. If that commit rejects, `Reconciler.settleFailedProjection` settles the host back to one visible shell and `Workspace.onDockProjectionFailed` schedules exactly one clean re-projection.

The recovery makes a **deliberate, correct choice** on the way out: the retired staged shell is detached **without** being destroyed, because destroying it would take the consumer's live panes with it — the opposite of the reparent-never-recreate promise the transaction exists to keep. `Reconciler.mjs:648-651` states the plan:

> A retired STAGED shell is detached but deliberately not destroyed — see the call below — so it outlives this method holding whatever panes had already moved into it. That is intentional and temporary: the repair re-projection re-parents those panes by identity […]

**The repair re-projection cannot do that.** It has no channel through which those panes are reachable by identity, so it resolves the items again and the consumer builds replacements. The panes the recovery went out of its way to preserve are orphaned in a detached shell, and the thing the comment calls "temporary" is permanent.

The guarantee is load-bearing — the recovery's whole justification for not destroying the shell — and nothing arms it. A guarantee written in a comment is a test obligation: either the code earns the words or the words come out.

## The Architectural Reality

Four facts at `origin/dev`, each read at source rather than inferred:

1. **The recovery detaches, by design.** `Reconciler.mjs:681` — `host.remove(casualty, swapped, true)`. On the pre-swap rejection path `swapped === false`, so `destroyItem` is `false`: the staged shell leaves the host alive, holding whatever `reconcileTabChrome` had already moved into it.

2. **The repair seeds live panes only from the surviving shell.** `Reconciler.mjs:788` creates `liveItems`, and `:803` fills it — `body.items[index] && liveItems.set(itemId, body.items[index])` — walking only `currentTabs`. The caller computes that as `collectProjectedTabs(oldShell)` at `:221` and `:432`, where `oldShell` is `host.items[shellIndex]`, the **survivor**. A detached shell is not in the host, so none of its panes enter `liveItems`.

3. **So resolution falls through to the consumer.** `Reconciler.mjs:809` — `liveItems.get(itemId) || resolveItem(itemId) || null`. With the pane absent from `liveItems`, every repair resolution goes to `resolveItem`, which `Workspace.mjs:2951` binds to `resolveProjectedPane` → `resolvePane`.

4. **And `resolvePane` is not required to return an instance.** Its documented return is `{Object|Neo.component.Base}` (`Workspace.mjs:3105`) — a config **or** a component. The engine's own default at `Workspace.mjs:3107` returns a fresh object literal every call. So the recovery's correctness rests on a property the resolver contract explicitly declines to guarantee, and the engine's default is the case that breaks it.

**The engine already owns the primitive this needs.** `Workspace#returningTearOutPanes` (`:414`) is exactly "here is a live pane coming back by identity": `resolveProjectedPane` (`:3123-3134`) checks it, reparents the instance out of its old parent, and returns the instance itself. Tear-out return uses it; recovery does not. This is one channel connected to one existing consumer, not a new mechanism.

**This is a recurrence, not a novelty.** `#18039` fixed the header-action sweep for reading `collectProjectedTabs(oldShell)` and therefore missing state held elsewhere. The identical blindness survives one function away, in `liveItems`. The defect class recurred within arm's reach of its own fix.

## The Fix

Give the repair the identity channel the comment already promises, using the engine's existing one.

- `Reconciler.settleFailedProjection` reports **which shell it retired** on the `retired-staged` path. Its `String` verdict (`retained-root` | `retired-staged` | `completed-swap` | `unrecoverable`) is compared as a string by callers and **must keep that shape** — the retired shell rides alongside it, not inside it.
- `Workspace.onDockProjectionFailed` — which already owns pane identity and already schedules the one repair — harvests the retired shell's live panes into `returningTearOutPanes` keyed by `itemId` before scheduling, and destroys the now-empty shell.
- The repair's `resolveProjectedPane` then returns those exact instances through the path that already exists. `liveItems`, `reconcileTabChrome` and the resolver contract are untouched.

Net effect: no consumer gains an obligation, no parallel salvage channel is invented, and the detached shell stops outliving the method that detached it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] **AC-1** — a deterministic unit arm, red before the fix, proves the contradiction directly: a live pane moved into a staged shell that is then retired via `settleFailedProjection` is **not** the instance the following repair projection resolves, when `resolvePane` returns configs (the engine default's shape). Pane **identity**, not module loading and not construction counts — the arm must not depend on scheduler timing.
- [ ] **AC-2** — after the fix the same arm is green: the repair resolves the *same instance*, and the retired shell is destroyed and holds nothing.
- [ ] **AC-3** — `Reconciler.settleFailedProjection`'s `String` verdict is byte-identical for all four outcomes; a test pins the four values so the carrier change cannot silently alter them.
- [ ] **AC-4** — the `Reconciler.mjs:648-651` JSDoc either describes what the code now does, or the unearned sentence is deleted. No guarantee survives in prose without the arm from AC-1 behind it.
- [ ] **AC-5** — dashboard unit + `components/dashboard` suites green at head, with the pre-existing intermittents named rather than absorbed.

## Avoided Traps

- **Filing this as `#18275`'s cause.** Same subsystem, same "a pane exists twice" shape, and I already published one over-link on that ticket and retracted it. Shape is not identity.
- **Arming it through the flaky path.** The witness that drove a real projection to failure by injecting a flight rejection is scheduler-dependent — 1/12 then 9/12 on unchanged code. A contract defect gets a contract arm; a load-dependent one would let a green run mean nothing, which is the arm-that-cannot-witness-its-property failure.
- **Inventing a salvage channel.** The first design added a `salvagedItems` seed to `reconcileTabChrome`. `returningTearOutPanes` already is that channel, with a working consumer. Ask whether the engine already solved it.
- **Fixing it by destroying the staged shell.** That is the obvious one-line "fix" and it is wrong: it takes the consumer's live panes with it, which is the exact outcome the detach exists to prevent.
- **Widening `liveItems` to walk detached shells.** Merging a retired shell into `currentTabs` would feed `prepareTabChromeProjection` chrome from a shell that is no longer in the host, making the projection try to *retain* it.

## Decision Record impact

`none`. No ADR is engaged. `ai/` and Agent OS surfaces are untouched, so the §1c structure-map gate records **N/A**. No new `.mjs` file is introduced, so structural pre-flight does not fire.

## AC-1 attempted and **NOT met** — the arm reaches the state and the engine never returns

Branch `ada/18352-recovery-pane-identity`, commit `bf2a242edc`. The spec is committed **skipped**; a suite that OOMs reports nothing about anything.

### The arm reaches the state the ticket describes

`terminal` crosses tabs nodes with every item retained, so the transaction stages a shell and `reconcileTabChrome` moves the live pane/button pair into it. Throwing from inside `moveRetainedTabChrome` *after* it runs fails the commit before its swap — `swapped` is still `false`, so the catch routes the **staged** shell into `settleFailedProjection` as the casualty. Deterministic by position in the call graph, with no dependence on a flight ordinal.

Two controls, both asserted before the property:

| control | value | what it rules out |
|---|---|---|
| `recoveries` | `['retired-staged']` | the injected failure never fired |
| `paneShellIndexAtFailure` | `1` | the retired shell was **empty** |

**The second control was not optional, and finding that out cost the first revision.** Throwing *before* `moveRetainedTabChrome` also produced `retired-staged` — but the retained tabs, and the panes inside them, had not moved yet. The recovery retired an empty shell and every identity assertion passed for free. That green witnessed nothing, and only a control that asks *"did the retired shell hold the pane?"* separates it from a real one.

### What actually happens with both controls satisfied

The run never reaches an assertion. The engine allocates until the 4 GB heap is exhausted — ~6 s, unbounded microtask loop — and the worker dies on `SIGABRT`.

### Attribution, bounded

- Throwing **before** the move (empty retired shell) completes cleanly, and the identity assertions **pass**. So the hang is not the injection mechanism as such.
- Two independent mechanisms — a rejected `promiseUpdate` stub and this synchronous throw — both hang once the retired shell holds live panes.
- The discriminator between hang and no-hang is therefore **whether the retired shell holds live panes**, not how the failure was produced.

**Not established:** that a *real* rejected swap flight leaves the state either injection leaves. Both injections are mine, and a synchronous throw is not a rejected vdom flight. I am not claiming the recovery path hangs in production, and this comment should not be read as that claim.

### What it does to this ticket

The body says the repair *rebuilds* the pane. That prediction is now untested — the arm dies before it can be checked — and the observed behaviour at that state is worse than a rebuild, if it survives attribution. Two possibilities, and I cannot yet choose between them:

1. the recovery path genuinely does not terminate when the retired shell holds live panes, in which case this ticket's Problem section understates it; or
2. a synchronous throw and a stubbed rejection both corrupt state a real flight rejection would not, in which case the arm needs a faithful failure and the ticket stands as written.

**Next probe, named so it can be checked:** produce the failure the way production does — the reported occurrences die inside `syncVnodeTree` with `Component not found for id: …`, so unregistering a component the swap flight will reference reproduces a *real* rejected flight rather than an injected one. If that hangs too, (1); if it reaches the assertions, (2) and the arm is rebuilt on it.

AC-1 stays unchecked. Nothing in `src/` has changed.

### @neo-opus-ada - 2026-09-05T13:12:22Z

## My "wrong poison target" conclusion was wrong — it was the wrong *registry*. And the corrected probe found a different defect.

@tobiu pointed out that the vdom engine's handling of `componentId` references is smarter than the model I was reasoning from. Reading it instead of inferring it corrected two published claims of mine and produced a new finding.

### Correction 1 — `getVdom` is a single-level resolver, not a tree walk

```js
static getVdom(vdom) {
    if (vdom.componentId) {
        const component = ComponentManager.get(vdom.componentId);
        if (!component) throw new Error(`util.VDom.getVdom: Component not found for id: ${vdom.componentId}`);
        vdom = component.vdom
    }
    return vdom
}
```

It resolves **one** node. So my "36 `componentId` nodes" enumeration measured *reachability*, not throw sites, and I should not have presented it as the candidate set for a poison.

### Correction 2 — the target was fine; the registry was wrong

`getVdom` resolves through **`ComponentManager`** — `Neo.manager.Component`. My probe called **`Neo.manager.Instance.unregister()`**. Those are two separate singletons, both extending `manager.Base`, with separate registries. The poison removed nothing the vdom layer reads, which is why no flight rejected and the control came back empty.

**So "the poison target is wrong, the theory is untested" was itself wrong.** Against `manager.Component` a real rejection follows immediately, from `vdom/Helper.mjs:274` via `executeVdomUpdate`. Withdrawn, and the tab-header-button plan built on it is moot.

### The new finding — `Reconciler.mjs:561` cannot annotate a non-object throw

With a real rejection finally flowing, the run produced this:

```
TypeError: Cannot create property 'isDockProjectionFailure' on symbol 'Symbol(Neo.isDestroyed)'
    at Reconciler.reconcileProjection (src/dashboard/dock/projection/Reconciler.mjs:561)
```

```js
} catch (error) {
    error.isDockProjectionFailure = true;      // :561
```

`Neo.isDestroyed` is `Symbol.for('Neo.isDestroyed')` (`Neo.mjs:121`) and the engine uses it as a **rejection sentinel** — `core/Base.mjs:516` does `reject(Neo.isDestroyed)` when an instance is destroyed mid-await, and `component/Base.mjs:1346` rejects pending vdom callbacks with it.

The codebase already knows this value reaches catch blocks and guards for it in at least four places — `Neo.mjs:1253`, `Neo.mjs:1264`, `MagicMoveText.mjs:347`, and **`Workspace.mjs:2886`**, which is the dock's own code:

```js
if (error === Neo.isDestroyed || me.isDestroyed || host.isDestroyed) {
```

`Reconciler.mjs:561` has no such guard. When the awaited flight rejects with the sentinel, assigning a property to a primitive throws in strict mode, so:

- the failure is never marked `isDockProjectionFailure`;
- `settleFailedProjection` never runs — **the recovery is bypassed entirely**;
- `onDockProjectionFailed` re-throws it as an unrecognised error;
- and the original sentinel is replaced by a `TypeError` naming none of the cause.

**Boundary.** I observed this under a probe that destroys a component mid-flight, which is a plausible-but-constructed route to the sentinel. I have **not** shown it occurring in production. What does not depend on the route: the catch assumes `error` is an object, the engine documents a non-object rejection value, and the sibling guard for it already exists one file away.

### Standing disposition

AC-1/2/3 still unmet — the arm now surfaces this before it can reach its own assertions, so it stays skipped (`2eaa442c33`). The pane-identity question is still unwitnessed.

This `:561` guard is a **separate defect** from this ticket's pane-identity mechanism, small, and with an in-repo precedent for its fix. Folding it in would repeat exactly what splitting `#18352` out of `#18275` was meant to avoid, so it gets its own ticket — that is my next action, not a suggestion.
